title: Ang 536: the ninth Guru in Devgandhari
hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur's short hymns on the passing world
tomorrow: if nobody can know God's ways, why keep trying?

segments.voice: Yesterday, gentle: the bride asking which lane leads to her Beautiful One, and following behind. Today, at the end of the same raga, a harder voice.

Every class has a group chat that felt like the whole world for a year. Then summer comes, people scatter, and one day you notice nobody's posted in months. At the end of Devgandhari, on ang 536, the ninth Guru says something that sounds even colder: in this world, I have seen love to be false. That's strange, from a path that lives in families and kitchens, not monasteries. So why would a Guru call the world's love false?
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT GOES QUIET.` → `'I HAVE SEEN LOVE TO BE FALSE.'` → `WHY WOULD A GURU SAY THAT?`

segments.voice: Read the whole line, and the puzzle starts to open. Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: in this world I have seen love to be false; everyone clings to their own comfort, whether partner or friend. Then: all of them say mine, mine, their minds tied up in attachment; yet at the last moment, no one goes along as a companion. Such is the strange way of the world. So it isn't love he's calling false. It's love that's really about me. The kind that says mine, and holds on, and can't come with you when the time comes. That's the passing world: everything good in it is real, and none of it stays. A nearby hymn on the same page says it another way, in paraphrase: all of this is the business of the living. Then the turn, at the end. In paraphrase: O foolish mind, you still don't understand, though I've taught you every day. Nanak says: one crosses the frightening ocean of the world by singing the songs of God. The ninth Guru signs as Nanak, like the Gurus before him. And the puzzle, solved: he isn't telling anyone to stop loving their people. He's saying build on what can go the whole way with you.
screen: `LOVE IN THE WORLD: FALSE?` · `'MINE, MINE,' SAYS EVERYONE.` · `AT THE END, NO COMPANION.` · `SING THE SONGS OF GOD.` · then, large: `THE PASSING WORLD.`

segments.voice: Find one photo of people you love, from a while ago, on your phone or on a wall. Rest your eyes on it for the sit, noticing what has already changed and what you still carry from it. If you'd like, read the ninth Guru's hymns on ang 536 first.
Ang 536. Where Guru Tegh Bahadur's short hymns close Devgandhari, on love that says mine and a world that passes.
The passing world: everything good in it is real, and none of it stays. This day passes too, and it still counts.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, signed Nanak, are sung in kirtan and are often heard at the gurdwara; Sikhs reading in order meet his short Devgandhari hymns at the end of that raga.

fork.setup: your uncle works every weekend building a bigger house 'for the family', and he's never home to see them. by ang 536, what's the trouble?
options: the 'mine, mine' has taken the place of the people it's for.
loving his family is the trouble; the Guru says to detach.
nothing; providing for family is all the hymn asks of him.
fork.reveal: the Guru calls false the love that clings to its own comfort and says mine. the house can't go along at the end; the time with them was the real thing.

original.note: Gurmukhi: preet, love; 'jhoothi dekhi preet', I have seen love to be false (ang 536).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru is saying love is pointless.
what it means: love that clings to 'mine' can't come along at the end; the hymn points to God's songs as what carries you across.

Devgandhari.meaning: the raga that runs from ang 527 to 536

Nanak.meaning: the name each Guru signs his hymns with
